YouAreRunningProguardWithoutAdministrato: You are running ProGuard without administrator rights, so you can only change processes you own. Rules can't touch system programs or programs you couldn't change yourself, and Purge now, clearing the log, Realtime priority and High I/O priority need administrator rights. Restart ProGuard as administrator to lift these limits.
TheCpuLimiterHasTakenCores: The CPU Limiter has taken cores away from this process for now

StandingOrdersAppliedEveryTimeA: STANDING ORDERS, APPLIED EVERY TIME A PROGRAM STARTS
PinAProgramsPriorityCapIts: Pin a program's priority, cap its CPU, keep it on certain cores, shield it from ProGuard's balancing, or stop it from running at all. Right-click any process and choose Make a rule, or start one here.
ProbalanceWontLowerItsPriorityEven: ProBalance won't lower its priority, even under load.
EndedTheMomentItStartsIncluding: Ended the moment it starts, including copies running now.
StartedAgainWithItsLastCommand: Started again with its last command line whenever it exits.
ACeilingWindowsEnforcesOnThe: A ceiling Windows enforces on the program.
TakesCoresAwayFromTheProgram: Takes cores away from the program while it hogs the CPU, then gives them back. Leave the threshold empty to switch it off.
WhichLogicalProcessorsWindowsPrefersFor: Which logical processors Windows prefers for the program. A preference, unlike core affinity.
TakeAwayAnyCpuSetsThe: Take away any CPU Sets the program has.
NewerCopiesOverTheLimitAre: Newer copies over the limit are ended.
OtherwiseOnlyCopiesInTheSame: Otherwise only copies in the same Windows session count.
SplitsTheCoresBetweenRunningCopies: Splits the cores between running copies of the program: an equal share each, or a fixed number each.
HandOutOnlyTheFirstThread: Hand out only the first thread of each physical core.
ThenThePriorityGoesBackUnless: Then the priority goes back, unless something else changed it meanwhile.
OnSteersItToTheEfficient: On steers it to the efficient cores. Off keeps it on the fast ones.
TakesEffectTheNextTimeThe: Takes effect the next time the program starts.
PutsTheseSettingsBackIfSomething: Puts these settings back if something else changes them.
WindowsStartsTheProgramWithIts: Windows starts the program with its priority, I/O and memory priority already set, instead of a moment later. Plain program names only.
HowTheEngineBehavesChangesApply: HOW THE ENGINE BEHAVES. CHANGES APPLY THE MOMENT YOU MAKE THEM.
WhenTheMachineIsOverloadedBackground: When the machine is overloaded, background hogs get their priority lowered so whatever you're using stays responsive. Restored the moment things calm down.
RestrainOnlyThroughTheExtraActions: Restrain only through the extra actions below
TakesOneCoreAwayFromThe: Takes one core away from the process while it is restrained
CoresARestrainedProcessMayUse: CORES A RESTRAINED PROCESS MAY USE
OnSmtMachinesOneThreadPer: On SMT machines, one thread per physical core
SetsThePowerPlansCoreParking: Sets the power plan's core parking minimum to 100% so no core sleeps while a hog is held back, and puts it back afterwards.
PauseProbalanceWhenTheMachineIs: PAUSE PROBALANCE WHEN THE MACHINE IS IDLE
TheWindowYoureWorkingInRuns: The window you're working in runs one step above normal priority, and drops back when you switch away.
EverySoOftenBackgroundProgramsAbove: Every so often, background programs above the threshold give idle memory back to Windows. Useful on machines short of RAM; unnecessary on most.
LogPassesThatFindNothingTo: LOG PASSES THAT FIND NOTHING TO TRIM
PurgeTheStandbyListWhenFree: PURGE THE STANDBY LIST WHEN FREE RAM IS LOW
OnlyWhilePerformanceModeIsOn: ONLY WHILE PERFORMANCE MODE IS ON
AlsoFlushTheSystemFileCache: ALSO FLUSH THE SYSTEM FILE CACHE
TrimsWorkingSetsAndPurgesThe: Trims working sets and purges the standby list (and the file cache, if switched on)
WhenYouveLeftTheKeyboardAnd: When you've left the keyboard and mouse alone for a while, switch to a lower-power plan. Your plan comes back the moment you return.
JumpsToAFastPowerPlan: Jumps to a fast power plan and puts your previous plan back when you turn it off. It can switch itself on while a game runs.
OnAutomaticallyAListedProgramOr: ON AUTOMATICALLY — A LISTED PROGRAM OR A GAME IS RUNNING
AlsoSetThePowerModeTo: ALSO SET THE POWER MODE TO BEST PERFORMANCE
YourPowerModeComesBackWhen: Your power mode comes back when Performance Mode ends. Windows uses it only under the Balanced plan, so pick Balanced above for this to count.
ProgramNamesOrFullPathsWith: Program names or full paths, with * as a wildcard. Performance Mode is on while any of them runs.
DetectGamesFromWhereTheyreInstalled: DETECT GAMES FROM WHERE THEY'RE INSTALLED
FollowsTheCpusLoadAFast: Follows the CPU's load: a fast plan while it's busy, a calmer one while it isn't.
AtLowLoadGoBackTo: AT LOW LOAD, GO BACK TO THE PLAN FROM BEFORE
InsteadOfSwitchingToTheLow: Instead of switching to the low-load plan, return to whatever plan was active before the switcher went high
SwitchWindowsPowerPlansByHand: Switch Windows power plans by hand, and choose the one to start with.
HowOftenWindowsClockTicksA: How often Windows' clock ticks. A finer timer makes sleeps and frame pacing more precise, at the cost of more wake-ups and battery. The engine holds it while it runs.
TheCoarsestTheTimerRunsAt: The coarsest the timer runs at (Windows calls it the minimum resolution)
TheFinestTheTimerCanBe: The finest the timer can be asked for (Windows calls it the maximum resolution)
Windows11HonoursATimerRequest: Windows 11 honours a timer request only for the program that made it. This switch (GlobalTimerResolutionRequests) makes requests system-wide again. Takes effect after a restart.
HowProguardFitsIntoYourWindows: How ProGuard fits into your Windows session.
ThisWindowHasStandardRightsSo: This window has standard rights, so ProGuard refuses Realtime and High I/O priority, Purge now, CPU tuning and the timer resolution. The engine keeps running either way; restarting only reopens this window, on this page.
ProguardAsksForAdministratorRightsA: ProGuard asks for administrator rights (a UAC prompt) each time it starts, including at sign-in, so Realtime and High I/O priority always work. Say no and it opens with standard rights. The installer turns this on for everyone unless told not to; this switch is your own choice.
PriorityIOAndMemoryPriority: Priority, I/O and memory priority, efficiency mode, cores and CPU caps you set on the Processes page are kept in that program's rule, so they are set again whenever the program starts, and put back if the program changes them. Windows' own processes stay one-off. Off: changes last until the process exits; use Always in the right-click menu to keep one.
StartsProguardInTheTrayWhen: Starts ProGuard in the tray when you sign in. The engine runs on its own either way.
ClosingOrMinimisingTheWindowHides: Closing or minimising the window hides it to the tray instead. Quit from the tray menu.
SaveTheRulesWatchdogRulesAnd: Save the rules, Watchdog rules and every setting under a name and switch between them, or move them to another PC as a file. A switch keeps what it replaced as BEFORE SWITCH.
WriteTheConfigurationInForceTo: Write the configuration in force to a file you can import on any PC
ShowsWhatTheFileWouldChange: Shows what the file would change before anything is applied
NoProfilesYetSaveTheCurrent: No profiles yet. Save the current configuration to start one.
CpuSetIdsCoresThisPc: CPU Set IDs, cores this PC doesn't have and power plans that aren't installed only make sense on the PC they were saved on: they are left out when a profile or file is applied, and the preview lists each one.
IfThisHappensDoThatChecked: IF THIS HAPPENS, DO THAT — CHECKED EVERY FEW SECONDS
TellProguardWhatToDoWhen: Tell ProGuard what to do when a program misbehaves: drop a CPU hog to idle once it's been pinning the machine for 30 seconds, end a memory leak at 4 GB, or just log it.
ItHasToHoldThisLong: It has to hold this long without a break before anything happens.
PerProgramOnceItHasFired: Per program. Once it has fired, it fires again only after this long or once the condition has cleared.

Rule_NeedName: Name the program the rule is for, e.g. chrome.exe.
Rule_BadPriority: Priority {0} isn't a Windows priority class. Pick one of the priority buttons.
Rule_NeedCore: Pick at least one core, or switch off "Keep it on certain cores".
Rule_BlockAndKeep: A rule can't both block a program and keep it running. Switch one of them off.
Rule_BadThreshold: The CPU Limiter threshold is a percentage above 0 and up to 100, e.g. 40. Empty it to switch the limiter off.
Rule_BadOverFor: The CPU Limiter's "over for" time is a whole number of seconds, 0 or more.
Rule_BadCoresToRemove: The CPU Limiter can remove 1 to {0} cores on this {1}-thread machine.
Rule_NeedCoreToRemove: The CPU Limiter needs at least 1 core to remove.
Rule_BadDuration: The CPU Limiter's duration is a whole number of seconds, 1 or more.
Rule_BadCpuSets: CPU Sets has to be a comma-separated list of CPU Set IDs. Use Pick to choose them.
Rule_BadMaxInstances: Max instances is a whole number of 1 or more. Leave it empty for no limit.
Rule_BadCoresPerInstance: Cores per instance is a whole number from 1 to {0}.
Rule_BadReserved: Reserved cores is a whole number from 0 to {0}: at least one core has to stay free for the instances.
Rule_OneCoreNoReserve: There is only one core, so none can be reserved.
Rule_BadMinCpu: The minimum CPU is a percentage from 0 to 100.
Rule_BadBoostPriority: Startup boost priority {0} isn't a Windows priority class. Pick one of the buttons.
Rule_BadBoostSeconds: A startup boost lasts 1 to 3600 seconds.
Rule_BadIo: I/O priority is 0 (very low) to 3 (high). Pick one of the buttons.
Rule_BadMemory: Memory priority is 1 (very low) to 5 (normal). Pick one of the buttons.
Rule_BadGpu: GPU priority is 0 (idle) to 4 (high). Pick one of the buttons.
Rule_BadGpuPref: GPU preference is 0 (let Windows decide) to 2 (high performance). Pick one of the buttons.
Rule_LaunchNeedsPlainName: Priorities at launch need a plain program name such as game.exe: Windows can't match a pattern or a path there.
Rule_LaunchNoRealtime: Windows doesn't apply Realtime priority at launch. Pick another priority, or switch off "Set at launch".
Rule_LaunchNeedsSomething: "Set at launch" needs a priority, I/O priority or memory priority to set. Pick one, or switch it off.
Rule_NoCpuSets: Windows reports no CPU Sets on this machine.
Rule_DeleteWarning: {0} goes back to running however Windows starts it. Processes already running keep their current settings.
